overview:
What replaced Yugoslavia in February 2003 was less a country than a holding pattern. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia — by then only Serbia and Montenegro, the last two republics still joined after the wars of the 1990s — had been left with a federal government that Montenegro's leadership under Milo Đukanović increasingly refused to take seriously. Podgorica had broken with Slobodan Milošević in the late 1990s, adopted the German mark and then the euro as its currency, and run its own customs and economic policy. Brussels, worried that another Balkan secession would encourage Kosovo and unsettle Bosnia, pushed the two sides into the Belgrade Agreement of March 2002, brokered largely by the EU's foreign policy chief Javier Solana. The Constitutional Charter that followed, ratified on 4 February 2003, retired the name Yugoslavia after some seven decades and created a confederal State Union with a single president, Svetozar Marović, a 126-seat assembly, and shared authority over little more than defence, foreign affairs, and minority rights.

Almost nothing about it worked as intended. The two republics kept separate currencies, separate customs regimes and separate economies; the union's institutions were split between Belgrade and Podgorica; the assembly struggled to legislate, and the EU eventually had to negotiate association terms on a "twin track," treating the two economies as distinct in practice while insisting they were one state in principle. The union's early months were violent — Serbia's reformist prime minister Zoran Đinđić was assassinated in March 2003 by figures tied to organised crime and the security services, a killing that stalled Serbia's post-Milošević reckoning. And the Charter carried the seed of its own end: after three years, either republic could call a referendum on independence. Montenegro did, on 21 May 2006, under rules the EU had set through its envoy Miroslav Lajčák — a 55 percent supermajority of valid votes, with turnout above 50 percent, a threshold Montenegro's government accepted only reluctantly. Turnout reached about 86 percent, and independence carried with 55.5 percent, roughly two thousand votes above the bar.

The vote split the country along lines that had been visible for years: overwhelming yes votes in the old Montenegrin heartland around Cetinje and in Albanian- and Bosniak-majority municipalities such as Ulcinj and Rožaje, heavy no votes in the Serb-identifying north near the Serbian border. International observers, including a large OSCE/ODIHR mission joined by parliamentary delegations, judged the process broadly in line with international standards. Montenegro declared independence on 3 June 2006; Serbia's parliament acknowledged the outcome two days later and declared Serbia the state union's legal successor, inheriting its seat at the United Nations and its treaty obligations — including, awkwardly, the unresolved question of Kosovo, which was still under UN administration and would declare its own independence less than two years later.
significance: This was the last act of Yugoslavia, and it ended without a shot — which is the point. Every previous separation from the federation had been contested by force or by siege; this one ran through a negotiated charter, a three-year waiting period, an externally supervised ballot and a losing side that conceded. The episode also showed the limits and the leverage of EU mediation: Brussels succeeded in delaying Montenegrin independence by four years and in setting the terms on which it happened, but could not manufacture a functioning joint state out of two governments that no longer wanted one. The 55 percent threshold became a much-cited precedent in later arguments about what majority a secession referendum ought to require, and Serbia's designation as sole successor set the legal frame in which the far harder Kosovo question would be fought out from 2008 onward.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all beneath the story, so the account above comes entirely from reference works and the referendum record rather than from anything the map can plot. The documentary record for the union itself is unusually good — the Charter, EU negotiating positions and international observation reports are all public — but it is thin on the union's internal workings, since the joint institutions did so little that few histories examine them closely; the internal Serbian politics of the period, especially the aftermath of the Đinđić assassination, are treated here only in passing.
